philippines-irrigation-canal-easement-re.title: 35 families moved off irrigation canal land, and 19.7 hectares signed over by 299 others, on ten Philippine irrigation systems
philippines-irrigation-canal-easement-re.place: Ten national irrigation systems, Philippines, with the resettlement sites in Region 5 (Bicol) and Region 11 (Davao), and the largest group of canal-easement households on the Tigman-Hinagyanan-Inarihan River Irrigation System in Camarines Sur
philippines-irrigation-canal-easement-re.point: Calabanga, Camarines Sur, one of the four municipalities the Tigman-Hinagyanan-Inarihan River Irrigation System runs through, per that system's resettlement action plan of August 2008. Point from OpenStreetMap. The completion report places the resettlement sites only in Region 5 and Region 11 and names no site and no coordinates.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P088926, Participatory Irrigation Development Project, loan 7709-PH (IBRD-77090). Loan agreement conformed 7 August 2009. The completion report of 25 April 2019 gives approval on 24 June 2009, effectiveness on 3 November 2009, a mid-term review on 10 May 2013, an original closing date of 31 March 2015 and actual closing on 31 August 2018, after four restructurings (11 February 2015, 24 September 2015, 31 March 2016 and 13 February 2017). The loan was US$70.36 million at approval, revised to US$58,015,957, all of which was disbursed; the borrower put in US$42,844,004, against US$43.23 million planned, and total project cost was US$100,859,961 against US$113.59 million planned. Environmental category: Partial Assessment (B). On safeguards the report says: "Overall, the NIS did not pose large-scale adverse social and environmental impacts, but pertinent safeguards policies were triggered, including Involuntary Resettlement (Operational Policy or OP 4.12), Indigenous Peoples (OP 4.10), Safety of Dams (OP 4.37), Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01), and Pest Management (OP 4.09)." The word "including" is the report's own, so this may not be the full list; the appraisal document's checkbox table does not survive in the Bank's text version of that document. The report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and the quality of monitoring Modest, and rates overall safeguards performance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review, filed by the Bank under 21 June 2019 and carrying no date on its own face, agrees on outcome, Bank performance and monitoring, and rates the quality of the completion report Substantial.

companies.name: National Irrigation Administration
companies.role: Implementing agency. A government corporation attached to the Department of Agriculture that builds and runs the Philippines' national irrigation systems and collects irrigation service fees; its Right of Way Management and regional irrigation offices handled the land acquisition, and the project also paid for the staff reduction under its own Rationalization Plan.

philippines-irrigation-canal-easement-re.community: The project rebuilt 58 national irrigation systems. Land had to be acquired on ten of them. The Bank's completion report counts 960 families: "a total of 960 families, consisting of 401 landowners, 288 informal settlers and 271 owners of crops trees that had encroached into existing canal right of way." Of the informal settlers, "35 families (13 are IPs) have availed of the resettlement sites that NIA and host Local Government Units (LGUs) have provided while the rest opted to relocate on their own or set back their homes from the canal after receiving cash compensation." The borrower's own annex to the same report puts those resettlement sites in Region 5 and Region 11 and says 299 project-affected people handed over 197,767 square metres, about 19.7 hectares, of right of way by deed of donation. Of the 401 landowners, who lost an average of 708 square metres each, 102 took compensation at the prevailing market price and the rest donated their land. The report records "some initial delays in the payment of compensation due to lack of legal supporting documents from claimants and different documentary requirements for the various types of tenurial status", says these "were all settled", and says funds for three absentee claimants were put in a trust account. It says the feedback from landowners who donated was generally positive, and the borrower's annex says living conditions improved, especially for those moved to the resettlement sites. On one system, the Tigman-Hinagyanan-Inarihan River Irrigation System in Camarines Sur, the resettlement action plan of August 2008 counted 204 informal-settler households inside the works area across four municipalities, of whom 45 wanted plots at a project-provided relocation site. No document found reports how many of those 204 were moved.
philippines-irrigation-canal-easement-re.outcome: The project closed on 31 August 2018. The completion report of April 2019 and the Evaluation Group's review treat the resettlement as finished and rate safeguards performance Satisfactory. Neither document says what the 35 families were paid, where the resettlement sites are, or what became of the 204 households counted on the Camarines Sur system in 2008.

philippines-irrigation-canal-easement-re.displaced_label: 35 families relocated to resettlement sites provided by the irrigation agency and host local governments, 13 of them indigenous (World Bank completion report, April 2019)
philippines-irrigation-canal-easement-re.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 204 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The same number appears in the August 2008 resettlement action plan for one of the project's 58 systems, the Tigman-Hinagyanan-Inarihan River Irrigation System in Camarines Sur, as the number of informal-settler households scattered inside the works area of seven irrigators' associations. The completion report's own count of people moved is 35 families.
philippines-irrigation-canal-easement-re.confidence_note: The Bank's completion report, the borrower's annex to it and the Evaluation Group's review of it are the only accounts found, and the review takes its figures from the report, citing paragraph 84 for each. No independent report of this resettlement was found. The two readings differ: the report says 960 families of whom 288 were informal settlers who had encroached on the canal right of way, while the review says "There were 960 families that had encroached into the existing canal right of way" and says that of those, the ones who did not take a resettlement site "relocated on their own upon receiving cash compensation", dropping the report's alternative that they set their homes back from the canal. The documents call the land handovers voluntary donations recorded by deed, and report no complaint and no unpaid claim beyond the three absentee cases.

muntinlupa-sewage-plant-site-clearances.title: 21 families cleared off two sewage plant sites in Muntinlupa, and a house down during sewer digging in Cupang
muntinlupa-sewage-plant-site-clearances.place: Barangay Tunasan and Barangay Cupang, Muntinlupa City, Metro Manila, Philippines
muntinlupa-sewage-plant-site-clearances.point: Barangay Tunasan, Muntinlupa City, where the Tunasan sewage treatment plant was built on an 8,333 square metre lot on Buendia Street, per the resettlement completion report of 8 March 2017. Point is the barangay from OpenStreetMap; the documents give no coordinates. The Cupang plant site, 12,733 square metres on Manuel L. Quezon Road, is about six kilometres north.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P113844, Metro Manila Wastewater Management Project, loan IBRD 81620-PH of US$275 million to the Land Bank of the Philippines with the guarantee of the Republic of the Philippines, on-lent to the two Metro Manila water concessionaires. The completion report of 23 December 2020 gives approval on 15 May 2012, effectiveness on 19 October 2012, a mid-term review on 30 January 2014, an original closing date of 30 June 2017 and actual closing on 30 June 2020, after closing-date extensions on 14 June 2017 and 27 June 2019. All US$275 million was disbursed; the borrower's own contribution was US$142,114,000 against US$96.7 million at appraisal, and total project cost was US$417,114,000. The project was classified Financial Intermediary Assessment (F) for environmental purposes. The completion report says the project triggered the involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12 and rates both environmental and social safeguards Satisfactory. The Evaluation Group's review says the project triggered Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01) and Natural Habitats (OP 4.04) and was classified as a financial intermediary operation for environmental purposes, and separately that it triggered OP 4.12; the appraisal document's checkbox table of triggered policies does not survive in the Bank's text version of that document, so the full list is not read here. The report rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring Substantial; the Evaluation Group's review, filed under 17 November 2021 and carrying no date on its own face, agrees on outcome and monitoring but rates Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, giving as its reason "There were shortcomings in project design." The Muntinlupa subprojects were the Cupang plant (US$27.68 million), the Tunasan plant (US$16.95 million plus US$4.94 million for nutrient removal) and the 4.12 km Muntinlupa conveyance system (US$14.74 million), all three unfinished at loan closing.

companies.name: Maynilad Water Services, Inc.
companies.role: Concessionaire for the west zone of the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System and the proponent of the Tunasan and Cupang subprojects; it bought both plant sites, paid the people living on them and ran the resettlement, which the Bank's documents describe as carried out under the project's loan covenant.

companies.name: Land Bank of the Philippines
companies.role: Borrower of the Bank loan and the financial intermediary that on-lent it to the concessionaires; a state-owned bank whose mandate is lending to farmers and fisherfolk.

companies.name: Dragonhart
companies.role: Contractor for the Muntinlupa sewerage conveyance system, named as such in the land acquisition completion report of May 2018, which records it working with Maynilad and the design consultant on a trenchless pipe-laying option to avoid moving the people living under the Pasong Diablo bridge.

muntinlupa-sewage-plant-site-clearances.community: Two of the project's sewage plant sites had people living on them. The Bank's completion report says all the land was bought from willing sellers, "including the lot needed for the Tunasan and Cupang STPs, which necessitated the physical displacement of informal settler families", and that the procedures were complied with "including in the relocation of 21 informal settler families in Tunasan STP and in Cupang STP". Its footnote 28 splits that figure: Tunasan 14, Cupang 7. At Tunasan, the resettlement completion report of 8 March 2017 names the 14 households and says their structures were cleared after compensation was agreed and paid. They had no claim on the land: the report quotes the project's own entitlement matrix, "Affected squatters and other informal settlers will not be entitled to compensation for affected land but will be compensated for affected structures and other investments made on the land and relocation assistance." The replacement plots were sold to them, not given: a relative of the sellers parcelled a 2,999.67 square metre lot into 32 square metre plots at 2,000 pesos a square metre, 64,000 pesos a plot, to be paid off over ten years after two rent-free years, at 500 pesos a month for a 32 square metre plot and 1,000 pesos for 64 square metres, with no interest. Each household also got between 10,000 and 20,000 pesos from the landowner for its house, depending on the structure, physical transfer help worth at least 5,000 pesos in kind rather than cash, and labour to pull their houses down so they could keep the materials. Ten of the 14 were living on the new lot by June 2016; four were not, and the report names them: one family went back to Palawan, one rents near his work in Muntinlupa, one lives with his parents, and one is in Canada and passed his plot to his brother. A Bank due-diligence visit on 20 June 2014 found four things unresolved at the new site: water connections, electricity, safe access in place of a narrow easement, and copies of land titles. At Cupang, the resettlement completion report of 28 May 2014 says eight informal-settler households, 44 people, were displaced from the Arevalo-Cruz Estate, which Maynilad bought from seven siblings. Seven of the eight were paid 143,000 pesos between them for the shanties that were removed and signed affidavits of willingness to vacate; the eighth, whose father-in-law was sick and could not move, had a new shanty built less than ten metres away plus 5,000 pesos. They had been given a notice to vacate dated 14 October 2010 and 90 days to take their structures down; eight renters and nine tenants of an apartment on the same land were given three months' notice before demolition. Three years after that, on 25 April 2017, the news site Interaksyon reported that a house in Barangay Cupang collapsed at about three in the morning and two neighbouring houses were damaged, and that "Initial observations pointed to the possibility of ground subsidence as the sewerage project was removing soil nearby"; it named a contractor of Maynilad as doing the digging, said the contractor would shoulder the consequences, and reported that the barangay chairman halted the work for technical checks. No Bank document mentions that collapse, and no document found says whether the excavation was part of the Bank-financed conveyance system. At loan closing the Bank listed, as social safeguards business still outstanding on that conveyance system, a memorandum of agreement to be concluded "with the owner of the house affected by the Bayanan Pumping Station in Cupang, Muntinlupa"; the same report's appendix describes the same house as one that "will be affected".
muntinlupa-sewage-plant-site-clearances.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2020 with the Cupang plant 91.99 per cent built, the Tunasan plant 91.57 per cent built and the Muntinlupa conveyance system 90.48 per cent built. The Bank left three social safeguards matters for Maynilad to settle after closing, with six-monthly reports: the construction method at a Valenzuela pumping station, the agreement with the owner of the house at the Bayanan pumping station in Cupang, and negotiations with the landowner on the Tunasan influent line, failing which the line would be re-routed to a steel bridge. The resettlement completion report says the Tunasan households' water and power were restored and titles prepared; no later document was found on the Bayanan house.

muntinlupa-sewage-plant-site-clearances.confidence_note: The relocations rest on the Bank's completion report, two resettlement completion reports written by the concessionaire and disclosed by the Bank, and the Evaluation Group's review, which repeats the report's figure. No independent account of the relocations was found. Two figures for Cupang do not agree: the Bank's completion report footnote gives 7 families, and the concessionaire's Cupang resettlement completion report of May 2014 says "Forty-four (44) project-affected-persons belonging to the eight (8) informal settler-households of Arevalo-Cruz Estate have been displaced", of whom seven households were paid. Neither document explains the gap. The documents report that the people paid said they were satisfied, and at Cupang the report cites signed affidavits. The house collapse of April 2017 is reported by a news site and not by any Bank document, and nothing found ties the excavation to the Bank-financed works rather than to the concessionaire's other sewer work in the same city; it is given here with that gap stated.

manila-sewerage-site-clearances-san-mate.title: 23 households moved off two Manila sewerage sites, one group paid 60 days' wages to go
manila-sewerage-site-clearances-san-mate.place: Barangay Guitnang Bayan II, San Mateo, Rizal, and the Road 5 communal septic tank compound in Barangay Project 6, Quezon City, Philippines
manila-sewerage-site-clearances-san-mate.point: Barangay Guitnang Bayan II, San Mateo, Rizal, the 15,243 square metre lot where the North Septage Treatment Plant was built, per the abbreviated resettlement action plan of 4 March 2005. Point is the barangay from OpenStreetMap; the documents give no coordinates. The second site, the Road 5 communal septic tank in Barangay Project 6, Quezon City, is about 12 kilometres west.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P079661, Manila Third Sewerage Project, loan IBRD-73110 of Japanese yen 6,592 million, the equivalent of US$64 million, to the Land Bank of the Philippines with the guarantee of the Republic of the Philippines. The loan agreement for loan 7311-PH was conformed on 22 July 2005. The completion report of 28 December 2012 gives approval on 21 June 2005, effectiveness on 6 March 2006, a mid-term review on 10 March 2008, an original closing date of 30 June 2010 and actual closing on 30 June 2012, with restructurings on 25 June 2010 and 17 January 2011; US$40.56 million of the US$64 million was disbursed. Environmental category A. The report says the environmental assessment policy OP 4.01 and the involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12 were triggered; the Evaluation Group's review cites page 17 of the appraisal document for the same two. The report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory and risk to the development outcome Moderate. The Evaluation Group's review, posted 12 March 2015 per its own Date Posted line, rates the outcome Unsatisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and the quality of the completion report Unsatisfactory, and agrees only on risk. Among its reasons it gives that only one quarter of the planned treatment plants were operating at closure and that measured pollutant removal reached 1,415 tonnes a year against a target of 20,400.

companies.name: Manila Water Company, Inc.
companies.role: Concessionaire for the east zone of the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System, implementing agency for the project and the buyer of the San Mateo site; it wrote both resettlement plans and paid the households.

companies.name: Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System
companies.role: The state corporation that owns the Metro Manila water and sewerage assets and holds the concessions. It owned the Road 5 land, terminated the lease of one occupant in April 2008 for unpaid rent and because the project needed the land, and ran the relocation there.

companies.name: Land Bank of the Philippines
companies.role: Borrower of the Bank loan and, with the concessionaire, an implementing agency; a state-owned bank whose mandate is lending to farmers and fisherfolk.

manila-sewerage-site-clearances-san-mate.community: Eight sites were built on and two of them had people living on them. The Bank's completion report says in its social safeguards annex: "Two of the eight sub-project sites had occupants who were requested to relocate prior to land negotiations and project implementation." At the North Septage Treatment Plant site in Barangay Guitnang Bayan II, San Mateo, Rizal, there were "eleven (11) households (46 persons) ... who were allowed by the former owner to reside in the property"; when he sold it they were asked to go, and the concessionaire "prepared an ARAP and provided relocation assistance to all the displaced households." The plan of 4 March 2005 names them one by one; the heads of the families were former employees of the previous owner and the first on the list, a widow who sold at the public market and kept backyard pigs, had lived there since 1975. They were offered either housing on 24 hectares of the former owner's land in Montalban or a package of 18,000 pesos a family, which the law set at 60 days of the minimum daily wage of 285 pesos, or 17,100 pesos, plus payment for their houses at replacement cost, free transport and the right to take their building materials. The plan says they chose the second option because the money could start a small livelihood, and that some meant to go back to their home provinces in Luzon and the Visayas. It budgeted 198,000 pesos in assistance and 33,000 pesos in transport, and says the families would get at least 60 days' notice before demolition. At the second site, the Road 5 communal septic tank in Barangay Project 6, Quezon City, the completion report says there were 12 households on land owned by the sewerage system, that they "were considered non-poor", and that "they were issued notifications to vacate the property." The relocation was run by the sewerage system with an inter-agency committee that included the Presidential Commission for the Urban Poor and the Commission on Human Rights, and each displaced household was given the standard package of 22,500 pesos, which the report describes as 60 days of the daily minimum wage, plus free hauling of their belongings. The plan written for that site in March 2005 counted three families, not twelve, headed by a former employee of the sewerage system who had been there since 1983, a tricycle driver there since 1986 and his unemployed cousin there since 1987; it said their houses sat on top of the septic tanks, that this was a risk to them, that an authority to demolish would be sought from the mayor's office, and that they had been told in October 2003 to leave. The completion report also records that all eight sites needed land, that only one private lot was bought outright, and that the rest were handed over by local governments on conditions such as building parks and sports facilities and refurbishing government offices, which the Evaluation Group says may have cost more than buying land.
manila-sewerage-site-clearances-san-mate.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2012. The completion report rates environmental compliance Satisfactory and says environmental and social policies and procedures were complied with. The Evaluation Group's review of March 2015 rates the project's outcome Unsatisfactory and says the concessionaire "demonstrated lack of realism, during both preparation and implementation, regarding its ability to resolve land acquisition and community resistance issues in a timely manner (or even, in some cases, at all)", that some local governments never delivered land they had promised, and that several planned plants were dropped. Neither document says where the 23 households went or what became of them.

manila-sewerage-site-clearances-san-mate.confidence_note: The relocations rest on the Bank's completion report and on the Evaluation Group's review, which quotes that report page by page, so this is one account and not two. No independent report of either clearance was found. Two figures for the Road 5 site do not agree: the abbreviated resettlement action plan of 4 March 2005 names three displaced families, and the completion report says that "By the time the sub-project was identified to be implemented in 2005, there were 12 households illegally occupying the land." Neither document explains the gap. The plan for that site also gives a safety reason for the move, that the houses stood on a septic tank not built to carry them, alongside the project's need for the land; the harm recorded on top of the move is the notice to vacate, the demolition, and a payment set at 60 days of the minimum wage with no payment for land. For the San Mateo site, the plan records the families' own choice of the cash package. Neither document gives the date either group actually moved.

east-tsankhi-herder-displacement.title: Herders off the East Tsankhi coalfield: two households part-compensated, 17 given nothing
east-tsankhi-herder-displacement.place: East Tsankhi coalfield, Ulaan nuur valley, Tsogttsetsii soum, Umnugobi (Omnogovi) province, Mongolia
east-tsankhi-herder-displacement.point: The Tavan Tolgoi mining area in Tsogttsetsii soum, mapped as industrial land in OpenStreetMap. The remedial resettlement action plan places the East Tsankhi coalfield in the Ulaan nuur valley, 16 kilometres south-west of the Tsogttsetsii soum centre, inside a deposit covering 220 square kilometres; it gives no coordinates for the affected camps.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Project P108768, Mining Sector Institutional Strengthening Technical Assistance Project, credit IDA-44890 (C4489-MN) and grant IDA-H4110 (H411-MN), together SDR 5.72 million, the equivalent of US$9.3 million; the financing agreement was conformed on 7 October 2008. The completion report of 30 March 2017 gives approval on 26 June 2008, effectiveness on 4 May 2009, a mid-term review on 1 November 2011, an original closing date of 31 December 2012 and actual closing on 31 December 2015, with restructurings on 2 July 2012, 10 January 2014 and 30 March 2015; SDR 5.66 million was disbursed. Environmental category B. No safeguard policy was triggered at appraisal. The report says that "following conduct of a safeguards review of the project in 2013, OP/BP 4.12 (Involuntary Resettlement) was triggered retroactively as part of the Restructuring in January 2014. This was in respect of the earlier financing by MSISTAP of the pre-feasibility study for ETT's East Tsankhi coal mine. The relocation of two winter shelters had taken place in 2010 in connection with development of this mine and more resettlements were anticipated to take place as ETT's coal mining operations expanded (albeit notrelated to MSISTAP or the East Tsankhi pre-feasibility study)." The Evaluation Group's review puts it more directly: the policy "was triggered as a result of the relocation of two winter shelters by an activity financed by the project." The project then paid for the remedial resettlement action plan and the resettlement policy framework for the mine's operator. The report rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, risk to the development outcome Substantial, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Evaluation Group's review, filed under 22 December 2017 and carrying no date on its own face, agrees on outcome and risk, rates borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and keeps Bank performance at Moderately Satisfactory while saying the report's own rating "should have been Moderately Unsatisfactory" under the harmonised rules.

companies.name: Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi JSC
companies.role: State-owned operator of the East Tsankhi coalfield and a subsidiary of the state holding company Erdenes MGL, whose pre-feasibility study for the mine the Bank's credit paid for. The remedial plan says it had no unit responsible for resettlement, that "ETT is just beginning to address resettlement with very weak capacity", and that it "has focused mostly on the extraction and transportation of coal and ignoring key requirements for adequate resettlement such as cut-off date."

companies.name: Ministry of Finance of Mongolia
companies.role: Implementing agency for the credit, through the project implementation unit it housed; the steering committee was chaired by its State Secretary.

east-tsankhi-herder-displacement.community: The Bank's technical assistance credit paid for a pre-feasibility study of the East Tsankhi coal mine, and the Bank later decided that this made the resettlement at the mine its business. The remedial resettlement action plan it then financed, drafted in December 2014 by a Mongolian research centre and an Australian consultancy, says the mine area "was the herders' important pasture resource prior to the commencement of East Tsankhi mining operation in 2010." It counts 26 households hit by the mine: "A total of 26 households were impacted by displacement due to ETT company's Eastern Tsankhi mining operation, out of which 2 households received incomplete compensation for physical displacement, however, 17 households impacted by economic displacement have not received any compensation." Two households were moved by the operator and two by a different coal company, and five more were moved by that other company inside a five-kilometre belt; the plan counts nine households physically displaced in all and 17 economically displaced. Of the two the operator moved, both are named. One lost two winter camps, each with its own hand-dug well, and about 1,250 hectares of seasonal pasture; he was given two winter camps by the soum government and 15 million tugrug, and the plan says "The winter camp provided by the company did not have a water well, which makes the winter camp to be impossible to use; thus Erdenebileg's opportunity for herding the livestock for livelihood was limited and he now lives in the soum center." It adds that no inventory of his assets or income was taken at the time, so "whether 15 million tugrugs are adequate to compensate the loss occured has not been properly studied or estimated." The second lost a winter camp, a deep well, about 550 hectares of seasonal pasture, a hot-water facility and a hectare of planted land; he was given 30 million tugrug, a new deep well, a winter camp from the other company and 0.7 hectares from the soum government "after running around for a while". He told the drafters: "The company drilled the deep-water well, but there was no waterbed (old water well provided 5 tons of water per 15 minutes, but new well works for 20 minutes until it dewaters and we need to wait another 3 hours until to regenerate the water). After the displacement, nobody visited us; when we asked about the hot water facility, they responded that the request was submitted to the management, and already 2 years passed." The 17 households who lost summer and autumn grazing were left out of the operator's resettlement work altogether, and the plan lists 15 of them by name with the pasture each lost, from 14 hectares to 2,772 hectares; against 13 of those names it records "Out-migrated", one "Deceased", and one who lost his livestock and settled in a bag centre. One of them is quoted: "Before ETT started its mining operation, we used to stay throughout the summer and fall in the southeast of Ulaan Toirom. Since the mining operation started, it became impossible to stay the same area and we moved to Tsagaan Ovoo Bagh." The plan says the exclusion happened because only herders with fixed assets such as winter camps and wells were counted, no cut-off date was ever announced, and the summer and autumn pasture that fattens the animals was treated as nothing. Its evaluation section says: "The company chose one package of compensation and mainly forced the package to the affected persons, therefore affected persons' right to freely choose from various options was limited"; "Committed compensation package was not fully provided, implementation of the compensation was not monitored, and the livelihood support measures were not planned and implemented"; "The post displacement livelihood of the affected persons was not monitored and evaluated. The strategy was to provide the compensation and forget about the affected persons"; and that there is no grievance mechanism. It also notes that the coal haul road to the Chinese border was not considered at all, and that more than 100 households in Tsagaan-Ovoo Bagh, a former mine workers' village, would be affected by dust from the mine's tailings from 2015.
east-tsankhi-herder-displacement.killed_note: The remedial plan lists one of the 17 economically displaced herders, recorded only as Chimid, as deceased. It gives no cause and does not connect the death to the mine.
east-tsankhi-herder-displacement.outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2015. The remedial resettlement action plan and the resettlement policy framework were prepared and disclosed, both still marked draft, and the Bank treated the amended safeguards covenant as complied with on that basis. No document found says whether the 17 uncompensated households were ever paid, whether the hot-water facility was built, or whether the unusable winter camp was given a well. A cumulative impact assessment for the area, financed by a different Bank credit, was still unfinished when this one closed.

Draft Resettlement Policy Framework of Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi Company (RP1758 V2)
Project Appraisal Document: Mining Sector Institutional Strengthening Technical Assistance Project (P108768), Report No. 43857-MN
Financing Agreement, Credit C4489-MN and Grant H411-MN, conformed copy

east-tsankhi-herder-displacement.displaced_label: 2 households physically displaced by the mine's operator, in 2010 and 2011, both named in the remedial resettlement action plan (December 2014)
east-tsankhi-herder-displacement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 41 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. That number appears in none of the six project documents read here. The remedial plan counts 26 households affected by the mine: 2 physically displaced by the operator, 7 physically displaced by another coal company, Energy Resources, and 17 economically displaced and uncompensated. Only the 2 are tied by the documents to the operation whose pre-feasibility study the Bank paid for, and the Bank's completion report describes the harm as "the relocation of two winter shelters". The 15 named households whose pasture was lost are recorded as having out-migrated, which the plan treats as economic displacement rather than as relocation.
east-tsankhi-herder-displacement.confidence_note: Everything here comes from documents the Bank financed or wrote: the remedial resettlement action plan and policy framework paid for by the credit, the Bank's completion report and the Evaluation Group's review of it. No independent account of the East Tsankhi displacement was found; searches in English and Mongolian returned coverage of two other mines in the same province, Oyu Tolgoi in Khanbogd soum and Energy Resources' Ukhaa Khudag mine, including a 2013 complaint to the European Bank's accountability mechanism filed by herders from Khanbogd and Manlai soums, which does not concern this mine or these households. The plan is marked draft, says its own field study of August 2014 was done in a short time on a small budget, and says further information gathering is needed for a fuller evaluation. It is also the document that reports the shortfalls against the company that commissioned the work. The Bank's completion report, while recording the two relocations, adds that further resettlements as the mine expanded were "notrelated to MSISTAP or the East Tsankhi pre-feasibility study". The Evaluation Group's review attributes to Bank staff, not to a document, the statement that there were no other safeguards issues during implementation.

P117470-laguna-de-bay-additional-financi.note: The additional financing ICIJ files under P117470 is already on the map as the Rodriguez ecotourism case, written from the completion report that covers the original loan P070899 and the additional financing together; that card already names P117470 and the 397 families. The only document harvested under P117470 is a resettlement plan of 18 December 2012, and the cached text of it holds nothing but the disclosure banner and the number RP1392, so it adds nothing. No extend is offered.

P074591-second-ulaanbaatar-services.drop_reason: No count of people moved and no documented loss. The outcome document, the completion report of 30 October 2012, says the resettlement plan expected the project to affect 47 households and one kindergarten, and that "During project implementation, no major complaints were received and no official resettlement claims were addressed, but the number of PAPs increased significantly to about 200 HH. The reasons for the change in the numbers of PAPs are not documented, nor are any additional costs known." A count of people affected is not a count of people moved. The Evaluation Group's review of the same report repeats the 200 and says it "was unable to find any documentation on the reasons for this or on any additional costs involved". The 2004 resettlement plan's figures are all in the future tense: 48 affected properties of which 43 partially affected, 11 gers and 6 small houses to be moved inside reduced fences, and 5 properties to be acquired whose residents "will be displaced"; no outcome document reports that those five were taken. Checked in the outcome document as well: the lessons section's "some compensation had been done by PMU by amending of contracts" is compensation to construction contractors for price rises, not to residents; and the pilot house connections at Dambadarjaa, where 96 households were connected, 43 were still connected at closing, pipes froze and the State Inspection Department received residents' complaints about poor service in June 2012, records a service built badly, with remedies funded by the municipality, and no loss to identifiable people.

P098572-northern-negros-geothermal.drop_reason: The resettlement happened before the Bank was involved, and the Bank's money bought emission reductions rather than works. The only document in the harvest is a resettlement plan whose cover is dated 12 September 2000, revised, prepared by PNOC-EDC, in the future tense: "PNOC-EDC plans to develop the Pataan Sector of the Northern Negros Geothermal prospect". The harvest listed no completion report because the Bank's archive carries that document with no document type; it was found in the project's own document list and read for this drop. That completion report on carbon finance, dated 29 June 2012, says: "By the start of World Bank engagement, the project was already halfway in its implementation and was implementing a comprehensive Environmental Management Plan ... It was also implementing a resettlement program for the residents of the geothermal development block." On the outcome it says "At the time of the review, EDC had already implemented a resettlement plan", that the Bank's review "found that the resettlement package and process were consistent and fully compliant with the World Bank policy on resettlement", and that an evaluation report in the appraisal document "confirmed the satisfactory outcome of the resettlement program including 50% improvement of the real household income and the attainment of better living conditions". No count of people moved, no documented loss, and the move predates the Bank's engagement.

P074290-second-eastern-indonesia-transpo.drop_reason: No count of people moved and no documented loss. The outcome document, the completion report of 29 March 2012, says: "Twelve sub-projects involved land acquisition and resettlement. Only one required a full Land Acquisition and Resettlement Action Plan (LARAP) and for the rest a simple LARAP was produced. Land acquisition and resettlement were satisfactorily implemented. There was one sub-project that needed further remedial actions, for which the local government made an extra effort to prevent one project-affected person from becoming worse off as a result of the land acquisition activity. This was well implemented, and documented in the aide-memoires." The Evaluation Group's review repeats those sentences. Checked in the outcome document: it gives no number of households or people moved anywhere, and the one person named as at risk is recorded as kept from loss rather than suffering one. The land acquisition plans in the folder are in Indonesian and are plans: the full plan for the Mataram northern ring road counts 108 parcels held by 102 households and 11 small traders who "akan direlokasi" (will be relocated) to Pasar Rembiga; no outcome document carries those figures.

P125496-integrated-modern-agriculture.drop_reason: The harm in the folder belongs to a different, domestically financed project and happened before this credit. The outcome document, the completion report of 30 November 2021, says of involuntary resettlement: "Project activities on infrastructure improvement mainly rehabilitated existing facilities on their original land base. All the facilities supported by the project belong to village communities and no land ownership or related property rights changed hands." The resettlement document of August 2012 that the candidate sentences come from is a due-diligence review of the Baiyang River Reservoir Hydro-junction Project in Fukang, Xinjiang, which it describes as "a related project of the World Bank-financed Integrated Agricultural Development Project" with a gross investment of 363.2218 million yuan of which 30 per cent was state appropriations, 37 per cent self-raised funds and 33 per cent domestic bank loans. Its recorded outcomes are 2,454.5 mu of state-owned pasture occupied, affecting 25 households with 137 people, 600 mu occupied temporarily, and the demolition of the Tianhe Hydropower Station under a compensation agreement of 1 September 2010 for 5.01 million yuan. The same document says the four households whose cultivated land was in question sit above the reservoir's flood level, so "the demolition of residential houses has been avoided", and that of the station's 30 employees 11 under 45 were re-employed in the water resources system from November 2010 at an average income "almost the same as their former income", with 6 early retirements and 7 retirees paid under a 2010 city document, and that a survey of 18 June 2011 found the 30 "were highly satisfied". The Bank's credit was approved on 27 December 2013, after those payments.

P112918-thailand-highways-additional-fin.drop_reason: The works were never built. The outcome document is the completion report of 29 December 2013 for the Highways Management Project and its additional financing, filed by the Bank under the parent number P075173; the harvest for P112918 held only the resettlement plan, so the parent's report was fetched and read for this drop. It says: "Under the AF, social safeguards screening for all five selected national highway sections was done. Since the proposed widening of selected road sections was to be carried out within the established ROW, no land acquisition and no significant demolition and displacement of population was required. Therefore, no resettlement action plan was prepared. However, a Resettlement Mitigation Plan (RMP) was prepared to address the limited resettlement impacts within the ROW to 21 temporary shops, and temporary use of 2.4 hectares of land areas by three households for planting paddy and sugarcane. The RMP summarized the in-kind rehabilitation measures to be provided to the 24 affected households. The RMP was not implemented due to bid failures as noted above." The additional financing was cancelled after procurement failed on nine civil works contracts. One candidate sentence, "All of the displaced 5 persons realized that the road widening would benefit to themselves", is an artefact: the figure 5 is the page number printed between the two halves of that sentence in the 2009 plan.

P106262-bicol-power-restoration.drop_reason: No people-bearing count of relocation and no documented loss. The outcome document, the completion report of 30 June 2009, says: "On resettlement, full compensation was provided to all project-affected households. Of 47 households with 35 dwelling and related structures potentially identified for relocation and compensation, only 29 structures were actually valued, compensated and relocated in consultation with displaced persons. Notably, together with current entitlements, payment was made for outstanding ROW claims that had not been settled since the original construction of the affected transmission lines." Twenty-nine structures is not a count of people or households, and the same report records the old unpaid claims being settled rather than left. On the negotiations it says there were "some differences between TransCo and landowners on compensation levels that took close negotiation to resolve, but agreement was reached in a relatively short time with no substantive impact on project outcomes", and that the utility agreed to "full and immediate payment and compensation adjusted for increased land values owing to improvements". The Evaluation Group's review of 9 November 2009 repeats the 47-household expectation and says social risks "were minimized since only a few structures were relocated". The land acquisition plan of June 2007 gives a budget of 25.9 million pesos including 8.36 million for replacement cost of houses and structures and 13.87 million for crops and trees; those are plan figures and no outcome document reports what was paid under each head. The report also says "There were no fatalities reported during the project period."

P085080-vietnam-road-safety.drop_reason: The outcome document says there was nothing to resettle. The completion report of 15 June 2013 says: "The project triggered the Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12 safeguards), but safeguards implementation work (under A2) revealed there were no resettlement issues on the demonstration corridors. The review of potential social impact, based on detailed designs for the corridors, confirmed there was no land acquisition, resettlement nor compensation involved for any of the package or corridors." The report's own output table carries the same finding as a row: component B2, Resettlement, "No land acquistion, resettlement, compensation involved", Completed, 0. This is the road-safety project the round brief warned about: every candidate sentence filed under deaths is a road-fatality indicator, including the fatality rate per 100 million vehicle-kilometres falling from 13 to 5.1 and the discussion of police under-reporting of accidents.

P125863-mongolia-community-led-infrastru.drop_reason: The only taking was fence strips, and the document that reports it is the one that reports the work done. There is no completion report for this project in the Bank's archive, which holds auditing documents and implementation status reports; the outcome-bearing document is the resettlement action plan of January 2014, written for 2013, which reports completed actions. It says the road component "will entail the resettlement of up to 31 families" and then: "Officials of Municipality, District, PMU, author of road design and community leaders carried out inventories of affected fences. There is no loss of property, resettlement or relocation. Type of effect is moving fences back through 0.5m-2.5m." On compensation it says "most part of households refused to solicit compensation procedure because of small size of affected land of households", that five households whose affected land ranged from 6 to 30 square metres submitted documents and had their rates confirmed, that the contractor "Helped 22 households to move their fences and restore them after construction work", dug two pit latrines and prepared 14 garage foundations, and that "There was no complain from affected households". ICIJ's figure of 31 is this plan's count of households whose fences stood inside the construction site.

P115695-bayannaoer-water-reclamation.drop_reason: Land was taken, more than planned, but no household was moved and the documents record payment before acquisition. The outcome document, the completion report of 24 June 2019, says: "During project implementation, 53 hectares of permanent land were required and only 22 hectares of land were used temporarily. All resettlement policies were carried out consistent with the resettlement action plan and in compliance with the Bank Policy OP/BP 4.12. Compensation was paid to the affected families before the land was acquired." The borrower's annex to the same report gives permanent land acquisition at loan closure as 798.05 mu against 682.5 mu at appraisal and temporary acquisition as 325.9 mu against 2,015.9 mu at appraisal, and says "All settlers had received compensation, with the total resettlement compensation of RMB 5.7 million in the project. The social external monitoring indicated that the impacted household can recover regular livelihood and are generally satisfied about the resettlement arrangement." The resettlement plan of June 2010 says "as this project does not involve house demolition, there is no population affected by demolition" and counts 5 households of 22 people in Shawan Village, Shanba Township, affected by land requisition; ICIJ's 22 is that plan's people figure. The reprint check flagged 50.5, 32.5, 22 and 15.5 hectares as appearing in both the Evaluation Group's review and the appraisal document: the review is quoting the appraisal's expectations, which it marks as such, and its own outcome figures are the report's 53 and 22 hectares. This is a judgement call on limb (b): land was taken from identified households and the actual area exceeded appraisal by 115.55 mu, but no document records a loss on top of the taking.

P087153-xiaogushan-hydropower.drop_reason: A plan only, and the design removed the house relocation. The Bank's archive holds no completion report for this carbon-finance operation, only implementation status reports from 2012, a resettlement action plan and an indigenous peoples plan. The plan, dated March 2004, says: "The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has considered launching a loan to the Project and the Loan Agreement has been signed. Meanwhile, the World Bank has considered to provide part of the PCF for the project construction. The impact scope of the Project is rather small (only affecting six rural households and some 100 mu grazing land." On the transmission line it says the towers were arranged "to keep away from the residents' houses, thus, eleminate the house relocation", and that the diversion tunnel and underground powerhouse were chosen to cut the land take. The construction loan is the Asian Development Bank's; the Bank's money was a purchase of emission reductions through the Prototype Carbon Fund, approved in 2005. No document found reports what was actually taken or paid.

P117323-indonesia-power-transmission.drop_reason: The land taking was paid for by the utility and the outcome documents record no resettlement. The completion report of 30 April 2020 says the subprojects were chosen to avoid it: "During the selection of subprojects, prioritization was made on the substation expansion which would only use the PLN's existing land and not require new or additional land acquisition, and only few substations required land acquisition for the expansion." On the hydropower component it says "the PLN financed the Land Acquisition and Resettlement Action Plan (LARAP) from its own budget", and the project paid only for the feasibility study and impact assessment of that plant, which was never built under this project. The Evaluation Group's review of the same report says: "Four substations in Sumatra would be expected to require land acquisition, with no resettlement or impact on building structures ... During project implementation, land acquisition for only one substation, i.e., Lahat substation, and a number of transmission towers along the Lahat-Kiliranjao corridor that were financed by the PLN was required. Land acquisition was completed in compliance to the provisions of the LARAP", and notes that the completion report gave no information at all on the implementation of the resettlement policy. No count of people moved and no documented loss.

P090376-shanghai-agricultural-pollution.drop_reason: The outcome document says the resettlement never happened. The completion report of 18 December 2015 says: "For involuntary resettlement, an abbreviated action plan was prepared for the wetland sewage treatment system component. The English version was disclosed on May 6, 2009, and the Chinese version on April 30, 2009. No resettlement took place, however, as the location of the subcomponent was changed, so compliance was satisfactory." The report names three safeguard policies triggered at appraisal: environmental assessment, pest management and involuntary resettlement. No count of people moved and no documented loss.

P123994-indonesia-second-power-transmiss.drop_reason: The subprojects that needed land were dropped from the project. The completion report of 23 January 2021 says: "There were no substantial social issues during implementation as the physical activities were limited to upgrading and extending the number of transformers on PLN's premises. There are no involuntary land acquisition/resettlement issues, and no indigenous peoples resided in the subproject sites ... No other adverse social impacts were anticipated or realized." The Evaluation Group's review of the same report adds why: "Because of the cancellation of most of the substation projects in Group 2 and the PLN's decision to finance the construction of those two new substations using its own resources, the investment works consisted of the expansion and rehabilitation of existing substations on PLN's own premises; hence, there was no land acquisition or involuntary resettlement during project implementation." The land acquisition plans in the folder, including the two dated August 2016, are for substations the utility went on to build with its own money.

P080054-laos-rural-electrification-phase.drop_reason: No count of people moved and no documented loss. The outcome document, the completion report of 30 January 2013, which covers this project and the sibling number P075531 the Bank files it under, says: "No major or irreversible environmental and social impacts occurred under the project, and mitigation measures applied adequately mitigated negative impacts. Consultations were carried out adequately and prior to the commencement of civil works with affected people. Impacts on loss of land and other productive assets were adequately compensated as per RAP." It also says "EdL branch offices made agreement(s) with individual household according to the social safeguard framework and recorded the voluntary contributions" and, in the same paragraph, "No external review on EMP/RAP implementation was carried under the Project", though the project's own resettlement framework of May 2004 required an external monitor wherever more than 100 people were affected in a cluster. That is a monitoring gap, not a documented loss to identifiable people, and no document found gives a figure for land taken, compensation paid or households moved. ICIJ's row carries no displacement estimate for this project.
